title: The Simple Classroom
author: Blake Harvard
summary: Prompted by a student's comment that his class 'isn't necessarily easy, but it's simple,' Blake Harvard unpacks what makes a classroom simple: predictability (known rules and expectations), consistency (routines applied equally and reliably, not just present), organisation and tidiness (visual and auditory clutter competes with attention, citing research on workspace tidiness and schoolwork performance), all of which converge on the ability to focus. He argues simplicity and ease are entirely separate qualities, using the analogy of lifting 500 pounds, simple to describe, extremely hard to do, to explain how a simple classroom environment and simple, direct instruction can still demand serious cognitive effort and challenge from students. He connects the simple-classroom argument to novice-learner theory, arguing that students new to a subject learn best from simpler, more direct instruction because they need to devote working memory to content rather than decoding complicated task instructions. He closes by tying the whole argument to his upcoming book on memory processing and learning strategies, framing the simple classroom as the foundation that frequent, well-designed assessment of learning then builds on.
points: Harvard's central distinction, simple versus easy, uses the 500-pound analogy to argue a classroom can be maximally predictable and uncluttered while the actual cognitive demand on students remains high.
He cites specific research (Annes, Taylor & Hallock) on workspace tidiness and high-school performance to ground the claim that visual and auditory clutter measurably competes with student attention.
He connects simple, direct instruction specifically to novice learners, arguing students new to content need to spend working memory on the material itself, not on decoding complex task instructions.
He frames predictability, consistency, and tidiness as instrumental, not intrinsically valuable, they all serve the single downstream goal of enabling sustained focus on content.
quotes: I was recently told by one of my students that my class "isn't necessarily easy, but it's simple." And, I've got to be honest with you, it made my day.
It's not enough to have appropriate rules, procedures, and expectations, they have to be applied equally and routinely. If that isn't the case, the classroom loses its predictability.
The visual perception system in the brain can process a limited number of outside stimuli, which can compete for visual attention.
For the simple classroom, less (visual distraction) is more (attention to content).
Lifting 500 pounds is simple. Just pick it up. But is it easy? For the vast majority of human beings, the answer is a resounding no.
Students should be doing a lot of thinking; a lot of assessing and using their newly gained knowledge to answer questions, discuss problems, and think creatively.
